questions.question: What problem does `track item.id` in an `@for` loop solve?
options: It gives Angular a stable identity per item, so re-renders update only the DOM nodes that actually changed instead of recreating the whole list
It disables change detection for that list
questions.explanation: Without a track expression, Angular can't match old and new list items reliably, which can cause unnecessary DOM node destruction/recreation — track item.id fixes that, similar to React's key prop.

questions.question: What is the difference between a pure and an impure pipe?
options: A pure pipe only re-runs when its input reference changes; an impure pipe re-runs on every change detection cycle regardless
Pure pipes can only be used with signals
questions.explanation: Pipes are pure by default for performance — they skip re-computation unless the input reference actually changes. Impure pipes opt out of that optimization and can be costly if overused.

questions.question: What does `loadChildren` (or `loadComponent`) achieve in Angular routing?
options: It preloads every route eagerly at app startup
It splits a route (or feature) into its own code chunk, fetched only when a user navigates there
It disables routing for that path
questions.explanation: Lazy-loading routes keeps the initial JavaScript bundle small by deferring a feature's code until it's actually needed, improving initial load time.

questions.question: What should come before reaching for optimizations like OnPush, track, or lazy loading?
options: Nothing — apply all of them by default everywhere
Measuring an actual performance problem, e.g. with Angular DevTools' profiler
questions.explanation: As with any performance work, these patterns should target a measured bottleneck rather than being applied blindly, since some add complexity of their own.
